world: Teece is a board of nine panels, three by three, and everything that lives on it is a Teece, born with a number on each side and a firm belief that the bigger one wins. Four old gods hold its frame: Topus the top edge, Rightorious the right, Bottomor the bottom and Levt the left. The further right you go the newer everything gets, from the workshops of the Works to the smoking Badlands; the further left, the older, from the Hallowed North down through the Wildwood to the Gloaming, where the dead keep house. Above the top edge burn the Heavens, home of the sun and the storm; below the bottom edge lies the Pit, where the Devils keep their books. In the middle panel, where every extreme meets and fights, stands Middlemark, built over Gol’God’Oth, who was asleep down there long before anyone laid the board on top of him. Past the edges the World of Teece runs on, folding over on itself, and strange things wander in from the creases. By long tradition, whoever ends a turn four Teece ahead of everyone else is, for the moment, in charge.

basic.name: Basic
basic.blurb: The deck for a first game, and the plainest in the box. Every card does one thing, and each one teaches a single rule of Teece: aiming a strong edge, Flying and Ranged, Tokens and sacrifice, equips, magic and battlegrounds. Its numbers are honest and middling with no tricks behind them, so it wins by reading the board better than the other side, and struggles against any deck that changes the rules underneath it.
basic.lore: The Common Levy of Middlemark: farmers, porters and apprentices from the streets and fields of the middle panel, where nobody has an ability and everybody has a pitchfork. Every war in Teece passes through Middlemark sooner or later, so the Footmen have fought for the Army, against the Ogres and under Knights who never learned their names. They sleep soundly, which in a city built over Gol’God’Oth takes real talent.
how: Point your strong edges. Only the two edges that touch are compared, and the smaller number is destroyed. The Footman is 6 on every side; the Shieldbearer, the Brawler and the Gatekeeper are strong on some sides and weak on others, so where you put them matters. The Pikeman has 10 on one side only, and may be rotated as it lands so you can aim it.

Movement and reach. Flying moves one space once per your turn: the Hawk Rider has it, and the Windcaller lends it with +2 for a turn. Ranged strikes the first enemy beyond the next panel and nothing strikes back: the Bowman has it, and lands with +3 for the turn.

Bodies and Tokens. The Conscript brings two Tokens beside it. Tokens never count toward winning and cannot be sacrificed, but the Captain and the General can only be played by sacrificing one or two of your other Teece; the General then calls a Soldier Token every turn. The Powder Carrier is weak, but every enemy beside it when it falls gets -8.

Cards that are not Teece. Equips (Iron Sword, Feathered Cloak, Longbow) go onto one of your Teece and stay. Magic is used once: Blink teleports a Teece and comes back to your hand the first time, Sway gives +3 or -3, and Waymark leaves a mark that pays the next ally to arrive +4 or the next enemy -4. Battlegrounds stay on a panel: Hilltop gives +3, Bog -3.

rats.name: Rats
rats.blurb: A swarm that wins by covering the board rather than by out-numbering it. Ten of the twenty cards are the same Rat, each one lets you play another for free, and every body in the deck gets +1 for every ally standing with it, so a hand goes down in a single turn and grows as it lands. Rats can never win by being four Teece ahead: they take the game the moment their Teece hold every panel, or by holding the most of the field when a deck runs dry. Brilliant on an open board; weak to anything that clears it in one go, and a razed panel shuts the main ending off for good.
rats.lore: Something is lurking in the drains under the Dump in the Badlands, the dark where progress throws whatever it has finished with, and there is a great deal of it. The Rats answer to the Rat King and his Queen and hold that any panel with a Rat on it is a panel improved. Every pipe from Middlemark and the Works runs down to them, so they hear everything the rest of Teece flushes away, and they have been gnawing their way back up those pipes for years. They share the dark with the Garbage, which they regard as lunch.
how: Each Rat you play opens the door for the next one, free of the turn's Teece play. Nine panels is the only thing that stops you.
Every Teece here reads the crowd: +1 for every other ally on the board, and the Rat King hands out another +2 on top of that. Swarmcloak pays +2 per ally to whoever wears it.

You cannot win by domination, so being four Teece ahead does nothing. Cover every panel with your Teece and the game is yours at the end of the turn; a razed panel puts that out of reach for good. Otherwise fill the board, stay filled, and take it when a deck runs dry — Swarm digs two Rats back out of the graveyard to keep that going.
The Rat King counts as two sacrifices, so it pays half of the Rat Queen on its own — and the Queen hands every Teece sacrificed for her straight back to your hand.

berserker.name: Berserker
berserker.blurb: Only twelve cards, and every one of them is bigger than it has any right to be: Titan is 16 on every side, Skullsplitter 15 on one edge, and even the smallest trade above their weight. The short deck is safe because Berserkers never deck out: your own empty deck does not end the game, only your opponent's does. The cards that are not Teece bring your dead back, to hand or to the board, so the plan is simply to hit hardest and keep hitting. It has little to say to silence, theft or tricks, and a thin hand can run out of bodies.
berserker.lore: The Berserkers are the cousins of the Runeblade tribe, who walked out of the Hallowed North the day the elders said the sword had to be shared. Twelve of them came south, and twelve has always been enough. They never run out because they never stop, and they hold a grudge against the Ogres of the Wildwood, who once shoved one of them.
how: Titan is 16 on every side and Skullsplitter is 15 on one — check which edge is facing you before you trade with either.
Warcamp sends your dying cards back to your hand instead of the graveyard, and charges an opponent two cards to break it.
Undying Axe comes back once a game: to your deck, or straight onto any panel you like.

rock.name: Rock
rock.blurb: Defence is the deck. Defence soaks up the difference in a fight, so a Teece with Defence 2 only dies to an edge that beats it by three or more, and almost every card here has some, hands some out, or turns it into attack. The Quarry Foreman, Studded Plate and the battlegrounds stack it up; the Rock Sergeant, Stoneheart and the Master Rock Flinger spend it as numbers, and Avalanche clears every enemy below a sacrificed ally. Slow to start and very hard to shift once built; weak to silence and to anything that destroys without fighting.
rock.lore: The Rock are the living stone of the High Mountains, children of the Rock God, the slowest and most patient of the Warlocks' patrons. They do not fight so much as decline to be moved. The Dwarves mine them, which they take personally; the Bombardiers of the Badlands blow them up, which they take very personally; and the Ogres throw them, which they have come, grudgingly, to enjoy.
how: Colossus is 10 on every side and destroys nothing at all unless your Master Rock Flinger is standing.
Master Rock Flinger pays every Teece on your side, itself included, +X where X is that Teece's own Defence, and gives it Flying.
Rock Sergeant pays an ally its own Defence as it lands, and Stoneheart pays its wearer +1 for each point it has — the deck stacks Defence, then spends it as attack.
Muckraider and Bedrock are immune to stat reduction, and cannot be selected by enemy effects.

ogre.name: Ogre
ogre.blurb: Shove everything, then make sure it cannot answer. Almost every Ogre moves a Teece as it lands, the penalties they hand out are permanent, and most of them Stun: a stunned Teece keeps its numbers but destroys nothing and uses no ability until the end of your next turn. The Trapper and the Tactician punish every enemy move however it happened, so your own shoves feed them, and Sinkhole and Concussion Alley make the panel itself the trap. Excellent at taking a built-up board apart; the bodies are only middling, and a Teece that cannot be moved, or is immune to stat reduction, shrugs off most of it.
ogre.lore: The Ogres live in the foothills between the Wildwood and the Mountains and serve the Ogre God, who is mostly a very large shove. Their great tactical insight is that a Teece that has been moved, hit and confused will not be doing anything for a while. They have a forty-year feud with the Army over who may move whom, they throw the Rock for sport and Goblins for distance, and Warlocks who channel their god come home with sore shoulders.
how: Stun is the deck. A stunned Teece cannot destroy anything and cannot use any ability — not even Flying — until the end of your next turn, which means it is useless for the whole of its controller's turn. The panel shows a burst badge, and a chip under the board names every stunned Teece on the field.
Ogre Trapper and Ogre Tactician punish movement however it happened, so your own shoves feed them — and the Tactician stuns on every enemy move for nothing at all.
Lumber is not March: ONCE while the body stands, not once a turn. The Chieftain and the Exploding Ogre each get one repositioning and then they are where they are.

Ogre Hexer is the answer to something that has been built up rather than something in the way: -2, silenced, stripped of every bonus, every equip destroyed, the battleground under it destroyed, and stunned.

Sinkhole destroys whatever moves onto it. Concussion Alley holds a stun on whatever stands there and lets go the instant it leaves — and anything that stuns a Teece already standing on it takes 4 off as well.

robot.name: Robot
robot.blurb: A flying factory. Every Robot has Flying, and nearly every one builds Drones as it lands, dies or stands: Tokens with 3 on every side that fly too. Drones never count toward winning, but they block, trade and pay: Swarm Node and Drone Tether grow them, the Chassis and the Data Centre grow on their deaths, and a Grey Goo Drone copies itself onto an adjacent empty panel at the start of each of your turns, every copy included, until the board is full of it. Strong at holding panels and at moving; the Robots themselves are only middling, so anything that sweeps Tokens away hurts it badly.
robot.lore: The Robots were built in the Works to do the jobs nobody wanted, and then they built the Drones to do the jobs they did not want either. A Gadgeteer left a batch of Grey Goo running over a long weekend, and the Drones have been copying themselves ever since. They fly because the road to the Badlands is covered in Garbage, and they keep well away from the Bombardiers, who keep asking to borrow some.
how: Drones are flying Tokens with 3 on every side, and Tokens never count toward winning: they are board, not lead.

Swarm Node and Drone Tether pay the Drones, Grey Goo builds one that copies itself at the start of each of your turns, and every copy does the same; Overclocker pays for movement instead, and Signal Relay wires the next three Drones to explode.
Factory Line can be paid with two Drones instead of a Teece, and a War Machine you cannot afford can be discarded for a Drone.

gadget.name: Gadget
gadget.blurb: Almost every card asks you to choose a mode, and the rest of the deck cheats that choice. Null Module, Preset, Coupling Rig, the Modular Platform and the Grand Apparatus make the next choice fire every mode at once or the chosen mode twice; the Safety Interlock locks every one of your choices to its first mode or its last; the Overdrive Engine grows and flies every time one resolves. The cards are small and flexible rather than strong, so it rewards a player who knows what every mode does and punishes one who just picks one.
gadget.lore: The Gadgeteers are the tinkerers' guild of the Works, engineers who believe there is no problem a sufficiently complicated tool cannot make more interesting. They built the Robots, the Overdrive Engine, and the Safety Interlock, which was meant to stop the Overdrive Engine and did not. They buy scrap from the Garbage, sell magazines to the Gun, and have not been allowed back into the Wizards' Tower since the Grand Apparatus incident.
how: Null Module, Preset, Coupling Rig and Grand Apparatus all bend the next choice: every mode at once, or the chosen mode twice.

Safety Interlock takes the choosing out of your hands: it locks every modality of yours to its first choice, or to its last. Played while a modality fires every mode, it locks both ends, and both fire every time.
Modular Platform sells the same trick as ground, and the size you give it decides which trick you get.

time.name: Time
time.blurb: Cards that grow or rot on a clock. Every Teece ages at the start of your turn: the Acorn, the Long Game and the Heir Apparent are next to worthless when they land and huge a turn or two later, while the Cut Flower, the Hourglass Knight and the Fading Titan, 30 on every side, start big and decay. Fast Forward, the Timekeeper, the Whetted Blade and Last Breath push clocks forward, the Chronoplate stops one dead, and Pause and the Stasis Field keep the growing ones alive long enough to pay. Strong in a long game; slow to start, and anything that kills a seedling before it ripens wastes the whole investment.
time.lore: The Clock Gardeners tend the Hours, a garden high in the Clockwork Heights where the world's clock is wound and an Acorn becomes an oak in two turns. They are kin to the Wildwood but trust nothing that grows at its own speed. They sold the Solar orders the Stopped Sundial and have regretted it ever since, and the Fading Titan is the last of the giants who ruled before anyone started the clock.
how: Acorn and Long Game are nearly worthless for two turns; then the Acorn comes up 10 on every side with +6 on top, and the Long Game 12 on every side.
Fast Forward, Timekeeper, Whetted Blade and Last Breath all push clocks forward — that is how you collect early.
Chronoplate stops a clock dead, which is what saves a Fading Titan. Sundial doubles it, which is only ever good on something growing.

witch.name: Witch
witch.blurb: Eight Hexes in place of equipment and battlegrounds, and twelve Witches that answer magic. A Hex can make a player lose a draw, silence their whole side, freeze them out of playing Teece, steal one of their Teece for a turn, or raze an empty panel off the board for good. Most Witches grow, fly, summon Familiars or silence something whenever you cast, so every Hex is also a growth spurt, and the Hex Collector, Hag of the Hollow, Witch Doctor and Witch Queen keep the spells coming back. Strong, steady control; the smaller Witches are fragile once the spells run out, and Hex of Freezing buys time rather than the win.
witch.lore: The Witches are the Wizards' sisters, who left the Tower the day it was decided that hexing a colleague did not count as scholarship. They brew in the Hollow, down in the Gloaming under Levt's patient eye, and trade Hexes to the Pixies for gossip. The Vampires and Zombies have learned to fight around the Hollow rather than through it. The Mummies' curses are older and cruder, and the Witches call them amateurs, loudly, from a safe distance.
how: Hex of Freezing is the trump: they cannot play a Teece at all, and you cannot win the game until it lifts — it buys time, not the win.
Most Witches trigger on you playing magic at all, so a cheap Hex is also a growth spurt.
Coven Matriarch turns every Hex of yours that picks one player into one that hits everybody — you included.

Hag of the Hollow fetches the hex you need when she lands, and when she falls she puts one back on top of your deck. Witch Queen and Witch Doctor want spells waiting in your graveyard and hand, so she keeps both of them fed.

bomb.name: Bomb
bomb.blurb: Area damage that does not care whose side it lands on. Mines on empty panels, Frag Charges, Cluster Bombs, Carpet Bombers and dying Shrapnel Troopers take numbers off everything in the blast, and the Chain Charge and the Overcharged Warhead make every Mine worse. The deck survives its own blasts with Blast Ward, which turns every loss on its wearer into a gain, and with the Blast-Proof Bunker and Siege Plating, which are immune to stat reduction. Brutal against swarms and crowded boards; careless placement blows up your own side, and the Unstable Warhead destroys itself the moment anything touches it.
bomb.lore: The Bombardiers serve the Bomb God, a patron the Warlocks rent from only in emergencies and only from a great distance. They were miners once, until they found that blowing up a mountain is faster than digging through it, and they moved down to the Badlands where nobody minds the craters. That made them the bitterest enemies of the Dwarves and of the Rock. The Avatar of the Nuclear Apocalypse is the Bomb God's idea of a sermon, and the Four Horsemen keep trying to take the credit for it.
how: Blast Ward inverts the whole deck: the Teece wearing it gains whatever it would have lost.
Mines sit on empty panels for -2 as anything arrives, and Chain Charge, Minefield and Overcharged Warhead all make them bigger.
Unstable Warhead destroys itself the moment anything targets it or takes a single point off it.

nature.name: Nature
nature.blurb: Plants that feed each other. Almost every card hands out a bonus, most of them permanent, and the Mother Tree, the Bramble Wall, the Ancient Redwood and the Creeping Ivy keep adding more, so the side grows all game. Hothouse Orchid and Sunlit Loam double the bonuses, and Sprouts pay +2 to every other ally when they die. The catch is the root: nearly every plant is soft on its bottom edge, so the panel above one is where it dies, and silence or a sweeping penalty undoes a lot of patient growth at once.
nature.lore: The Wildwood grows down Levt's side of the board, older than any road through it, and its plants feed each other because nobody else will. The Locusts eat them, the Garbage smothers them and the Pixies live in them rent-free; the Solar orders, warming them from the Heavens, are the only neighbours they actually like. The Knights ride through it as if they owned it, and the forest is very patient.
how: Nearly every plant is thin on its bottom edge — Sapling, Elder Willow and Mother Tree 1, Hothouse Orchid 0 — so the panel above it is where it dies.
Hothouse Orchid and Sunlit Loam double every positive effect, and the bonuses here are permanent, so they compound all game.
Plant Pot is +20 on the bottom side alone, which is exactly the edge the deck keeps leaving open.

pixie.name: Pixie
pixie.blurb: Tiny flying creatures with almost no numbers and an enormous amount of magic. Every pixie flies, and the deck keeps pulling spells out of graveyards, out of the deck and out of thin air, then bends the field with them: Mind Control takes a Teece for a turn, Enlarge and Shrink rewrite one, Invisibility and Pixie Projection protect, and Silence strips one for good. The Pixie Queen hands you a Queen's Enlarge every turn, and the Spellbound Pixie grows with every spell. The pixies are 0s, 1s and 2s, so it is very strong in skilled hands and falls over the moment the spells run out.
pixie.lore: The Pixies are children of the Fey, tiny, airborne and ungovernable, and they live in the canopy of the Wildwood, which is the reason a Warlock's Fey patron never answers on the first ring. They steal spells from the Wizards for fun and from the Witches for profit, and they once enlarged a Badlands drain Rat to the size of a cathedral, which is where the Rat King got his ideas. Nobody has ever caught one, because nobody has ever managed to hit a 1.
how: Pixies are 0s, 1s and 2s. They are not meant to fight — they are meant to keep casting.
Trickspinner, Wisp of Nothing and Enchantment conjure magic out of nothing; Thieving Sprite, Grave Pixie and Echo Pixie pull it back out of graveyards and decks.
Pixie Queen hands you a Queen’s Enlarge every turn (+10 until the start of your next turn), and is the one card that turns the swarm into a board.

spider.name: Spider
spider.blurb: A cannibal swarm on its own battlefield. The Web covers every panel but the corners from the first turn; a Spider Teece or Spiderling on it can Skitter one space a turn, and a Spiderling has +1 Defence there. The Spiders pour out Spiderlings with 4 on every side and then eat them to pay for everything else: the Spider itself, 10 on every side, costs one, Eaten Alive spends three to destroy any Teece, and the Brood Mother makes every Spiderling on the Web a 12. Spiderlings are Tokens and never count toward winning, so the deck needs real bodies to close, and the corners are where it is weakest.
spider.lore: The Spiders spin the Web that covers every panel but the corners, anchored in the Sinking Sands where the Brood Mother waits. They say they were here before the board, though not, they admit, before what sleeps under Middlemark. They are a cannibal brood that raises Spiderlings to eat them, they catch Pixies, they have a standing arrangement with the Cult (whose pentagram, they point out, is drawn on their silk), and they refuse to discuss the corners.
how: Spiderlings are Tokens, and Tokens never count toward winning: they are fuel and board, never a lead.
The corners are never Web, which makes them the one place a Spiderling gets neither Skitter nor its extra Defence.
Brood Mother reprints every Spiderling on the Web at 12 on every side — either side's — and stops them being sacrificed at all.

Spider is 10 on every side and costs one of your Spiderlings to play, and nothing else will pay for it. Broodfather and Brood Mother can be thrown away from your hand to summon a Spiderling, so a boss you cannot afford yet still feeds the swarm.

vampire.name: Vampire
vampire.blurb: They grow by taking. Drain X takes X off a Teece and gives the drinker exactly what it managed to take, so a Teece immune to stat reduction gives up nothing, and the Vampire Castle, the Transfusion Catalyst and Enhanced Fangs all bend the number on the way. The Fledgling, Nightstalker and Starveling drain as they land; the Nosferatu, the Elder, which drinks from every other Teece on the field, and the Transmogrifying Vampire, which turns from a Humanoid into a flying Bat and back, keep drinking every turn; Blood Bank doubles every drain in play. Mist Form is the trump card: an ally invulnerable for three of your turns, though it destroys nothing while it lasts. A plain beginner deck that wins long fights; the Parasite must drink every turn or die, and silence stops the bleeding.
vampire.lore: The Vampires are the Wizards' exiled dark sorcerers, banished to the Gloaming at the bottom left of the board, where they have spent ten thousand years at war with the Zombies over who gets to eat the living. Their Lord fell to the Runeblade, and the Elders still flinch at swords. They grow by taking, they mortgage their castles to the Devils next door, and they think the Zombies vulgar for eating the whole thing.
how: Parasite has to drain at least once on each of your turns, by any means, or it withers and dies. Its own bite only drinks from your side, but any other drain counts.
Enhanced Fangs doubles what you take. Vampire Castle and Transfusion Catalyst double everything either way, up and down alike.
Blood Bank doubles all Drains, both sides' and Suck's included, and two Blood Banks double them again.

zombie.name: Zombie
zombie.blurb: They come back when you kill them. X Undying Y means the card returns X times a game, each time Y stronger (or weaker) than the last, on any free panel you choose, so the Shambler grows and the Rotting Brute shrinks but is still a body. The rest of the deck works both graveyards: the Necromancer and Brief Return raise the enemy's dead, Back Again and Death's Avatar wind Undying counters back, and Plague Winds tilts the whole board by one every turn. Very hard to grind out; silence keeps a zombie down, and a returned body arrives with no protection, so placement is everything.
zombie.lore: The Zombies are the other army of the Gloaming, raised by Nagash, the necromancer-god the Warlocks rent from, who is the reason none of them will stay down. The war with the Vampires has lasted so long that both sides have forgotten the cause, though the Zombies suspect it was brains. The Mummies of the Sinking Sands are their snobbish distant cousins, and a Priest's Smite is the one thing they genuinely fear.
how: The return count belongs to the card, not the body, so bouncing a zombie back to hand does not launder it. Back Again and Death's Avatar are the two that wind it back.
Silence stops it getting up. A silenced zombie stays down.
Plague Winds hands every ally +1 and every enemy -1 at the end of every turn — both sides' turns, not just yours.

tictactoe.name: Tic Tac Toe
tictactoe.blurb: A second game laid over the first. Every Teece is an X, an O, or both, and three of one letter of yours in a straight line wins at the end of that turn, however far behind you are on bodies. The X and O Toerrains mark bare panels, the cOrpse, X-tinct and XOD leave Toerrains behind when they die, and the Oliminitator, Xecutioner, suppOrt and mediX grow with every letter on the field, whoever controls it. The bodies are tiny, so it lives or dies on reading lines: a body standing on your Toerrain blocks it, and a destroyed letter or a razed panel stops a line cold.
tictactoe.lore: Nobody knows where the Noughts and Crosses came from. The Planewalkers swear they fell out of a crease in the World of Teece, where the land is folded so tight it comes out in little grids. They care nothing for bodies, only for lines, and the Priests of the Four Sides note uneasily that three in a row along an edge looks a lot like a prayer to that edge's god. The Cult watches their lines with professional interest.
how: A body covers the ground it stands on, so standing on their Toerrain blocks that line instead of joining it.
The board lights up any line standing at two with its last panel still open, whoever holds it.
bOX and XOD count as an X and an O at once, which is two lines from one body.

solar.name: Solar
solar.blurb: The sun in the corner of the board becomes a moon at the start of every round, so your turns alternate between Day and Night. Half of what this deck prints is worth having in one half of the cycle and nothing in the other: by day it summons Solar Tokens and pays its allies, by night it silences, assassinates and takes numbers off enemies. Duskfall, Daybreak, Solstice and the Solar Tyrant turn the sky on purpose, and the Stopped Sundial stops the round turning it. Flexible and strong for a player who plans two turns ahead; awkward when the sky is wrong for the hand you hold.
solar.lore: The Solar orders tend the great sky that turns in the Heavens above Topus's edge, a sun one round and a moon the next, and they split long ago into those who serve the day and those who serve the night. Both halves share a deck because neither will let the other out of its sight. By day they warm the Wildwood and by night they hide their Assassins, and they blame every eclipse on the Clock Gardeners, who sold them the Stopped Sundial.
how: A card that only works in one half of the cycle tells you so when you play it in the other.
Equips read the sky too: Twilight Cloak is +3 Defence by night, and +7 with Flying by day.
Stopped Sundial stops the round turning the sky while it stands, though cards can still turn it. It never destroys anything itself.

army.name: Army
army.blurb: A deck paid for its shape. Almost nothing here is worth much standing alone: Teece gain numbers, Ranged, March and protection for standing beside an ally, and the equips pay for lines, corner triangles and a lone Teece in the middle. Brigadier Ryan and Brigadier Bryan call each other down and are +10 each side by side, Colonel Cornell pays everyone in his huddle, and Field Marshal Marshall makes every Teece count as adjacent to all of its allies, the enemy's included. Strong and simple to pilot; break up the formation, by shoves or one kill in the middle, and every number falls with it.
army.lore: The Grand Army marches out of the Clockwork Heights, drilled by Field Marshal Marshall in the belief that standing next to someone is a moral virtue. It recruits from the Common Levy of Middlemark, borrows horses from the Knights it insists it does not need, and has spent forty years in a border feud with the Ogres over who is allowed to move whom. Brigadier Ryan and Brigadier Bryan are not related, and are tired of being asked.
how: Beside means the four panels a side touches, never a diagonal. Line Formation is the only card here that counts diagonals, and it counts them as lines rather than as neighbours.
Brigadier Ryan and Brigadier Bryan call each other up: play one and the other may go down the same turn without spending your Teece play. Side by side they are +10 each.
Scout Stout is paid for having its back to the board — two sides on a corner, one side and Ranged on an edge, all four in the middle — so it wants the panel nobody else does.

garbage.name: Garbage
garbage.blurb: Twice the deck and twice the turn: forty-four cards, two Teece plays and two draws every turn. Nothing here is worth much on its own, and much of it pays by being thrown away: the graveyard is the stockpile, Living Dump, Trash King and the Dumpster read the heap behind you, and the Raccoon and the Garbage Man fish cards back out of it. The bigger turns flood the board with small bodies, while Rancid Mist and Living Smog sour the enemy and fire, rats and a shopping cart do the rest. Strong at out-numbering slower decks; every single card is weak, so one big body or a sweeper can stall it.
garbage.lore: Everything Middlemark and the Works throw away ends up in the Dump in the Badlands, and in Teece anything left lying long enough with a number on each side eventually stands up. The Garbage is led, loosely, by MucKing, and worships the God of the Forgotten, who is made of every card ever discarded. It shares the drains with the Rats, sells scrap back to the Gadgeteers, and once ate a Robot.
how: Two Teece a turn and two cards a turn are the deck's own rule, not a card's: they hold for as long as you are playing Garbage. Garbage Soul adds a third of each while it stands.
The graveyard is a resource. Living Dump grows with it, Trash King eats it for attributes, Garbage Man and Raccoon fish cards back out of it, and Banana Peel and the Dumpster spend it.
Fire sits on a panel rather than on a Teece. Anything standing in one has -4 while it burns, and it burns until the start of the turn of whoever lit it.

apocalypse.name: Apocalypse
apocalypse.blurb: The end arrives on schedule. The four Horsemen start on top of your deck, so they are your opening hand, and each one played can bring another out of your hand with it, silenced. The Harbingers turn the board against itself (War makes every Teece fight its own neighbours, Plague and Famine wear the enemy down), and the Trumpet and the Seal of Armageddon call the Horsemen back as Tokens. Everything after that is paid for in cards: Final Judgement and the River of Blood clear the field for discards, and the deck grows on every card that reaches a graveyard. Fast and wide early; it burns through its own hand to win, and a long game leaves it short.
apocalypse.lore: The Four Horsemen, Famine, War, Plague and Death, are not so much a faction as an appointment, and it is written on every calendar in Teece. They ride in from the far World of Teece, from every edge at once. Death rides for the Warlocks' patron of the same name, War hires itself out to the Army whenever the Army can afford it, and the Bombardiers keep trying to bring the date forward, which the Horsemen find unprofessional. The End Draws Near is not a threat, only a scheduling note.

madness.name: Madness
madness.blurb: Played out of the graveyard rather than into it. On your turn you may discard any card in your hand as often as you like, and almost every card here does its work on the way out: turning a Teece, making one invulnerable, +8 to a top, Teece that climb back out of the grave, spells that refill the hand. An empty hand is a win condition of its own: Astral Mindwyrm, the Goggles of Truth and the Paranoid Schizophrenic all pay for holding nothing, and the Echo of Gol’god’oth makes everyone throw their hand away. Enormously flexible for a player who sees the lines and baffling for one who does not; it runs through its cards fast.
madness.lore: The Mad are what is left of the Middlemark scholars who listened too closely to Gol’God’Oth through the floor. They throw away everything they hold because the voices say a full hand is a cage, and the worrying thing is that it works. Most of them were Wizards and Witches once; the Eldritch Library is the one the Wizards locked and lost the key to, and the Cult sends missionaries among them who mostly come back confused.
how: Discarding is free and unlimited on your turn. It is a rule of the deck, not of any card, so no card has to print it.
An empty hand pays: Astral Mindwyrm is +10, Paranoid Schizophrenic is +10 (Top 11, Right 12, Bottom 13, Left 14), and the Goggles of Truth add another +5 the moment anybody runs dry.
The Eldritch Library shelves discards as a wall of Defence instead of burying them, and the Pocket Dimension takes back everything you threw away this turn.

dimension.name: Dimension
dimension.blurb: Eight of its twenty cards are battlegrounds, and the twelve Teece only mean much standing on one. The panels do the fighting: the Dimension of Change swaps opposite sides, Multiplicities doubles printed numbers, Goo pins and silences, Pain rots, the Black Hole swallows everything beside it, and the Extradimensional Plane of Matter hangs a tenth panel off the edge of the board. The Riftwalker, Native of Nowhere, Shifting Architect and Eldritch Terraformer reward and rearrange the ground, and the Warden of the Threshold or a Dimension of Dimensions make it impossible to remove. Strong once the field is laid; a deck that destroys battlegrounds, or a draw of bodies with no ground to stand on, leaves it weak.
dimension.lore: Past the edges of the nine panels the World of Teece folds over on itself, crease after crease, and the Planewalkers who live in the folds treat the ground itself as a weapon. They first noticed the board when a careless Wizard opened the Extradimensional Plane of Matter, and they have been redecorating it ever since. The Fusion creatures crawl out of the creases they leave, and the Cult believes one of the folds runs all the way down to Gol’God’Oth.
how: Almost every body here reads the panel rather than itself: Native of Nowhere and Dimensional Anchor pay only on a battleground, and Riftwalker starts walking the moment anybody lays one.
Dimension of Dimensions is played ON another battleground: the two fold into one panel that cannot be replaced or destroyed, and it reaches one panel further out.
Black Hole Dimension eats every equip and every non-Boss Teece beside it and hands the lot back when it goes — and it goes on its own, at the start of your turn, once it holds three.

The Extradimensional Plane of Matter is played OUTSIDE the board, hanging off the left or right edge of a panel. It is a tenth panel from then on — a Teece stands on it and fights across the edge it hangs on — and it drifts round the board carrying whatever is standing on it.

locust.name: Locust
locust.blurb: A swarm that wins by filling the board with copies of itself. Every Teece you control has Flying, printed on the deck rather than the cards, and you can never win by being four Teece ahead: you win outright the moment every panel holds a Locust of yours. Half the deck answers being destroyed by putting more of itself down (the Nymph bursts onto every panel beside it, the Breeding Locust copies itself coming and going, the Carrion Locust digs the dead back up), and the Locus and the Hivemind arm the swarm once it is out. No two Locusts are the same shape and most are soft underneath, and a single razed panel puts the ending out of reach for good.
locust.lore: The Locusts come out of the Wastes in the far World of Teece once in a generation and eat everything until there is only Locust. They have no plan beyond the next panel, unless the Hivemind has one and is not saying. The Wildwood dreads them, the Rats resent the competition, and the Four Horsemen claim them as Famine's outriders, which the Locusts have not noticed.
how: The ending is the deck: a Locust on every panel takes the game as a turn closes, however far behind you are on bodies. The chip beside the board counts how many of the panels are yours — and warns you if one is ever razed off the board, because nothing can stand on a razed panel and that puts the ending out of reach for good. Raze and the Hex of Razing are the answer to this deck.

A copy does not fire its own when-played, so a Locust Brood fills four panels and stops. When-DESTROYED does fire, which is why the Locust Nymph chains — and why it is capped at three bursts a turn across every copy of it.
Everything flies, so the swarm can shuffle one space a turn to close the last gap, diagonals included.

The two Bosses are what the swarm is for: Locust Locus costs two bodies and arms the next four Locusts with +6 Defence, and the Locust Hivemind costs four and pays every Teece you control +3 for the rest of the game, buried or not.
A trodden Grasshopper leaves two Tokens with 6 on every side that can be sacrificed — the only spendable Tokens in the game, and half the price of the Hivemind on their own.

devil.name: Devils
devil.blurb: Devils are evil, but lawfully. Every Devil offers you a PACT as it lands, a price before the semicolon and a reward after it, and the choice is always yours: pay it, pay with a SOUL instead, or reject it and keep it on offer for a later turn. You start the game holding one SOUL, Soul Harvest and Brimstone Wings make more, and Soul Debtor's Prison lets you run up a tab once they are gone, paid back double if it ever falls. The Devils are solid numbers on their own and the bargains are optional, so it is gentle to start with; the steep prices (the Beginner Devil, the Adversary, the Infernal Bargain) are where it wins games and where it loses them.
devil.lore: The Devils run the Pit beneath the bottom edge as a commercial concern: evil, but lawful, and scrupulous about paperwork. Every PACT is binding, every SOUL is accounted for, and Soul Debtor's Prison holds half the Vampire aristocracy of the Gloaming for unpaid castles. They are the Warlocks' favourite patrons because the terms are always clearly printed, and they wrote the contract that made The Gun Devil, which they maintain was a misprint.
how: A PACT reads PRICE ; REWARD. When a Devil lands you choose: Accept PACT and pay the price, Pay with a SOUL instead, or Reject PACT. A rejected PACT is not lost: the Devil keeps a PACT button you can press once per turn until you take it.

You start with one SOUL, and the chip beside the board shows how many you hold. Soul Harvest makes another every time it is cast, and comes back to your hand if you feed it an ally; Brimstone Wings pays one out when its wearer dies.

The Seal of Exemption makes its wearer’s PACT free — plate it onto a Devil still in your hand and the PACT it offers on landing is already paid. The Sacrificial Altar offers a PACT of its own at the start of your turn to whatever of yours stands on it: sacrifice that Teece, and any Teece gets +X permanently, where X is the sacrificed Teece’s lowest stat.

Soul Debtor’s Prison: with no SOUL left, any price can go on its tab instead. When the Prison is destroyed, every price on it is paid twice. Whoever controls a Teece standing on it can break it on their own turn — your opponent included, so do not let them stand there.
The Infernal Contract lets a Devil offer its PACT again once a turn, and Devil Numbers renumbers any Teece to 6 on every side with one side at 0 before letting an ally offer its PACT again.
Beginner Devil’s PACT throws away your hand, your whole board and your whole deck for +1. Sorry, it’s new. Take it only when something else is paying.

runeblade.name: Runeblade
runeblade.blurb: One sword, and a tribe built around it. You start the game holding the Runeblade, an equip that adds nothing on its own, and once a turn it comes back to your hand from wherever it is. Almost every Teece reads it: the Runeblade Elder is +7 with it, the Sigil Hurler gains Ranged, the Skyleap Raider flies, the Hush-Seer silences everything beside it, the Blade-Waker stands it up as a flying Teece and Bladerang throws it through a line of enemies. Consistent and strong, since the key card never leaves you; but it is one sword, so stunning, stealing or bouncing its wielder slows the whole deck, and the Bladeless Exile pays for every turn the sword is out.
runeblade.lore: In the Hallowed North, an ancient tribe of nomadic warriors perfected their ancestral magic. Their greatest artefact is the Runeblade, the sword their whole culture has been built around for countless millennia, carved with thousands of tiny sigils by their ancestors and said to have slain the World Dragon, vanquished the Vampire Lord and felled the Leviathan. The Berserkers are the cousins who left, the Vampires still flinch at the sight of it, and the Dwarves have spent a thousand years trying to forge a copy; the Blade That's Close Enough is as near as they have come.
how: The Runeblade is one equip card. On its own it adds nothing; almost every Teece in the deck reads it instead — the Runeblade Elder is Top 1, Right 2, Bottom 2, Left 3 without it and gets +7 with it, the Sigil Hurler becomes Ranged, the Skyleap Raider flies, and the Hush-Seer silences and weakens every enemy beside it.

Once a turn, on your turn, the Runeblade returns to your hand from wherever it is: off a dead Teece in your graveyard, off whoever is wearing it, out of a Runestone, or up off the field when it is standing there as a Teece. The chip beside the board is the button. The Keeper of the Blade calls it back a second time.

Hand it on: the Blade-Waker stands the sword up as a Flyer with 8 on every side, Bladerang throws it through every enemy in a line and onto an ally, and the Grudgebearer bolts it onto whatever killed your last wielder — which is stunned for as long as it has to hold it.

Keep it alive: the Blade-Sworn Squire breaks the Runeblade to dodge its own death, the Decoy Runeblade dies in the real one's place, and The Runeblade’s Chosen makes its wielder invulnerable until the sword leaves the field.

Make more: The Ancestor-Smith forges a second Runeblade onto itself, and the Barrow Forge makes another every second time a wielder falls on it. The Bladeless Exile is the price of all this — huge, but -5 while any Teece anywhere holds the sword.
Ragnarok ends it: break a Runeblade for good, with its wielder, and two Teece of your choice go down with it. Or take Triumph, and the next Teece to take up the sword gets +5 and Flying for the turn.

wizard.name: Wizard
wizard.blurb: Advanced and complicated. Every Wizard conjures an element into your hand as it lands (Fire, Water, Wind or Earth, each a small spell), and two different elements combine for free into something stronger: Steam, Fireball, Lava, Ice, Mud or a Sandstorm Elemental. The Elementals grow on their own element, the Archmage makes every element stronger, and with a Grand Magus out all four fold into Holy. The bodies are small and the power is in a hand that never empties, so it rewards careful planning and punishes forgetting the hand limit of six.
wizard.lore: The Wizards are an ancient race who have shepherded every sentient being along the enlightened path of magic, from a Tower in the High Mountains nobody else is allowed to find. They purged their dark sorcerers long ago, exiling them to the Gloaming, where the Vampires and the Zombies wage their eternal war. With their Elemental helpers, and the reluctant help of their sisters the Witches and the trickster Pixies, they are the oldest and most respected masters of magic in Teece, and the only ones who know exactly how deep Gol’God’Oth sleeps.
how: Every Wizard conjures an element when it is played: Fire (a Teece gets -2), Water (+2), Wind (move a Teece one space) or Earth (a battleground with +3 Defence). Elements go straight into your hand as magic cards.

Two different elements in hand can be combined with the Combine button on the card, which costs no play: Steam, Fireball, Lava, Ice, Mud, or Summon Sandstorm Elemental (puts a flying token with 7 on every side and Defence 2 on the board, which leaves a Sandstorm when destroyed), each stronger than either half.
With a Grand Magus on the field, Fire, Water, Wind and Earth together combine into Holy: destroy a Teece and raise one of yours from the graveyard in its place.
An Archmage on the field makes every element stronger. The Elementals grow each time you play magic of their own element.
Elements count toward your hand limit of six, so spend or combine them before your turn ends.

gun.name: Gun
gun.blurb: Gain bullets, then spend them. Bullets are a count, not cards, and on your turn the gun comes out: every bullet is a permanent -1 on any Teece you point it at, up to six shots a turn. The rest of the deck feeds the gun (the Gunslinger, the Ammo Drone, the Bandolier, the Armored Ammo Truck), answers it (the Sharpshooter and the Shock Trooper react to every shot, the Bullet Sponge and the Kevlar Juggernaut want to be shot), or turns it into something worse: the Executioner finishes anything shot five times in a turn, and The Gun Devil fires in all eight directions as it lands. Simple to play, with precise damage anywhere on the board; it runs dry without its suppliers, and a Teece immune to stat reduction shrugs off the whole magazine.
gun.lore: The Gun rode in from the dusty Badlands, down in Rightorious's corner, with an invention nobody else had, and they have never stopped explaining it. They follow the Gun God, who is on no Warlock's list because he refuses to share, and buy their magazines from the Gadget guild in the Works. Zeus says he invented the bolt first; The Gun Devil was a contract from the Pit next door that went extremely wrong.
how: Bullets are a count, not cards: the Gunslinger, the Ammo Drone, the Armored Ammo Truck and others hand them over when played, destroyed, or discarded from your hand. Your count shows beside your name and on the gun chip under the board.
On your turn, tap the gun chip to take out your gun. The pointer becomes a crosshair: tap any Teece to spend a bullet and give it -1 permanently. Shooting costs no play. Holster it whenever you like.
The magazine holds six shots a turn. Once they are fired the gun is empty until the start of your next turn, unless something reloads it (Speedloader, the Armored Ammo Truck, the Ammo Drone dying).

Several Teece answer every shot: the Sharpshooter gets +1 for the turn, the Shock Trooper stuns the enemy that was hit, and the Executioner destroys an enemy shot five times in one turn. Headshot and Armor-Piercing Rounds make each shot at one Teece hurt more.

Shoot your own Teece when it pays: the Bullet Sponge gets +1 instead of -1, the Kevlar Juggernaut cannot lose stats and takes Ranged and Flying for the turn, and a Gun Range battleground grows +1 every time you shoot it.

The Gun Devil fires a bullet from your reserves in all eight directions when it is played, and whatever each one hits is destroyed, yours included. The Avatar of the Gun God takes your gun away and gives its wearer a -5 shot down its row and column instead.

fusion.name: Fusion
fusion.blurb: Twelve odd creatures that can become one. Every Fusion Teece has Fuse: two of them in hand fuse into a single card with both cards' sides added together and both cards' keywords, Defence and effects, and two standing side by side can fuse on the board once a turn, keeping every equip and bonus. The board counts bodies, so fusing trades two Teece for one far bigger one; the magic fuses anywhere on the board, makes a bonus permanent, or fuses two fusions into a Boss. Advanced, and very strong when the right pairs line up; fuse carelessly and you are a body short.
fusion.lore: Where two folds of the World of Teece press together there is a Space Between Spaces, a seam where the stuff of different places commingles and combines. The Fusion Teece emerge from it: strange combinations of different entities, the Chimera and the Shellephant among them, each one looking for something to become one with. The Wizards study them, the Pixies keep them as pets, and Hyperfusion is what happens when somebody leaves two of them alone in a room.
how: Every Fusion Teece has the Fuse keyword. On your turn, tap Fuse on one in your hand and pick another Teece in your hand that also has Fuse. The two become one card whose sides are the two added together, carrying both cards' keywords, Defence and effects. Play it as your Teece for the turn and both when-played effects fire.

Once per turn you can also fuse on the board: a Fusion Teece standing beside another of your Fuse Teece can use Fuse to become one body with it, on either of the two panels. Both bodies' equips and every bonus and penalty on them are kept. A Mergeling in the fusion adds +3.

A fusion is one card where there were two, and the board counts bodies, so fuse to win fights rather than for the sake of it. When a fusion is destroyed, every when-destroyed effect it carries fires, and the cards it was made of go to the graveyard separately.
A fusion does not fuse again. Hyperfusion is the exception: it fuses two fusions from your hand, your side of the field, or one of each, and the result counts as a Boss.
Contact Fusion fuses any two of your Teece anywhere on the board, with +2. Phase Drift teleports one of your Teece and gives it +5 for the turn, kept for good if it fuses that turn.

It That Stands Alone gives +5 to a Teece that is not a fusion, and Fusion Core gives +4 to one that is. Unstable Catalyst breaks and draws you 2 cards when its wearer fuses. The Fusion Chamber draws you 2 when a fusion is made on it, and the Space Between Spaces gives a fusion standing there +6.

lightning.name: Lightning
lightning.blurb: A swarm that floods the board faster than anyone. Thunder Twin, Spark Sprite and Last Light play more Teece out of your hand by effect, which costs no Teece play; Surge Rider, the Surge Coil and the Lightning Queen buy extra plays; and the Static Conductor, Stormwing and the Thunderhead Rig grow on every arrival. A few cards answer on your opponent's turn at instant speed: Counterstrike when they play a Teece, Static Counter when they cast magic, Zeus' Blessing when one of yours would be destroyed. Fast and aggressive, aiming at board domination; but a Teece summoned by an effect does not count toward domination until it has started a turn under your control, and the bodies are small once the burst is spent.
lightning.lore: The Stormborn are the children of Zeus, a sky god who lives in the Heavens above the top edge and is also, to his annoyance, a Warlock patron. They flash into being the instant something happens, which makes them the fastest faction in Teece and the worst at conversation. Zeus has a long feud with the Gun over who invented the bolt, and the Lightning Queen keeps a strained truce with the Solar orders, who share the sky, for the sake of the weather.
how: Playing a card by an effect is called a summon. It never costs the turn's Teece play, and a Teece that arrives by an effect from this deck counts as a Thunder summon: it does not count towards board domination until it has started a turn under your control.

Counterstrike answers any enemy Teece being played, and Static Counter answers any magic card your opponent plays: either one can be played straight from your hand the moment it happens. Zeus' Blessing answers a Teece of yours about to be destroyed on your opponent's turn, and the Teece survives.

Thunder Twin and Spark Sprite chain into more Teece from your hand, and Last Light and Spark Sprite replace themselves when destroyed. Flashstrike is a plain 5 until it arrives by an effect, then it is a 9.

Bolt Army puts three Bolt Tokens in your hand. They can be sacrificed to pay for the Lightning Queen or for Zeus, and each one lets you play another Bolt Token when it lands. Zeus calls a Lightning Bolt into your hand every turn, and the Bolt takes 6 off the highest Teece in whichever column you pick.
Capacitor, Surge Coil and Thunderhead Rig are plated onto a Teece while it is still in your hand. Storm Landing and Static Field turn the panel itself into a trap.

mummy.name: Mummy
mummy.blurb: A beginner warrior deck built on one curse, and the bandage that drags enemies onto it. Mummies curse panels and Teece; a non-Mummy that lands on a cursed panel picks the curse up, and a cursed Teece cursed again gets -1 instead. Every Mummy has Mummy Wrap, once a turn: a bandage fired up, right, down or left that pulls in the first Teece it hits (an enemy gets -2), or swings the Mummy to the wall if nothing is there. The Tomb Stalker, the Pharaoh, Pharaoh's Vengeance and the Cursed Tomb cash curses in for big penalties and kills. Simple and punishing at close range; Cleanse lifts curses, and silence turns the payoffs off.
mummy.lore: The Mummies serve Ankhtepot, a god-king who died in the Sinking Sands and has refused to accept it ever since, even as his tomb slides an inch a year toward the Pit. They wrap, curse and drag their enemies into the sand, and their curses are the oldest magic in Teece, older than the Witches' Hexes, a point the Witches dispute. The Paladins have sworn to Cleanse every curse they lay, the Zombies are the cousins they do not invite to dinner, and Warlocks who channel Ankhtepot come home with bandages in strange places.
how: Curse the empty panels first, then wrap. A bandage pulls its catch one space back along the line, so an enemy one step past a cursed panel lands on it and picks up the curse. Tomb Stalker charges -3 for every enemy moved onto a curse.

Each Mummy Wrap is once a turn. Tomb Stalker has two, Burial Wrappings adds two more to whoever wears it, Mummy or not, and Linen Mummy and Cursed Bandages pay +3 for the turn every time their Teece wraps. A bandage that hits nothing swings the Mummy to the wall, which is how a Mummy gets around.

Pharaoh’s Vengeance, Wrathful Mummy, Shifting Sands and Soul Steal all lift a curse as they cash it in, so the same enemy can be cursed fresh again: on the Cursed Tomb that is another -5, and with the Pharaoh’s order standing it is a kill.
Accursed Sands curses any non-Mummy standing on it, and curses it again the moment that curse is lifted. Mummies are never cursed by a panel, so your own side can stand on every curse you lay.

wolf.name: Wolf
wolf.blurb: A beginner swarm that fills the board from one card. A Pack Leader brings a Token copy of itself onto every free panel beside it, and when the leader leaves the field its copies go with it. Howl gives an ally +3 for the turn and Bloodlust, which teleports it beside an enemy; the Den Mother and the Wolf Pup lend numbers to the pack, the Pack Warden makes leaders invulnerable inside their packs, and the Dire Wolf and Fenrir can be paid for with the Tokens. Huge board presence early; the copies never count toward winning, and killing a leader takes its whole pack with it.
wolf.lore: The Wolves run in packs across the Hallowed North, between the camps of the Runeblade tribe and the Paladins' snowline chapels. Every pack is one wolf and its echoes, and when the leader falls the echoes fade into the snow. They come down into the Wildwood to hunt the Knights' horses, howl at the Solar moon, and get on well with the Berserkers, the only people in Teece who howl back.
how: Play Pack Leaders where the most panels around them are free: a Grey Wolf in the middle of an empty board is five bodies. The copies are Tokens, so they never count toward board domination, but they fight, they block, and they carry everything printed on the card except Pack Leader itself.
The copies keep their card’s text. A Den Mother’s copies give +1 to whatever stands beside them, a Wolf Pup’s give +3 and Bloodlust, and a Pack Warden’s copies count as a Warden too.

Kill the leader and the pack goes with it. With a Pack Warden out, a Pack Leader that has two or more of its own copies beside it is invulnerable, so thin the pack first; Alpha’s Collar adds +4 to one, and Wolven Promotion turns a copy into a new leader with a pack of its own that no longer depends on the old one.
Dire Wolf and Fenrir can be paid for with Tokens, so a pack is a Boss waiting to happen. Fenrir gives every other Teece you have Howl. Lone Wolf is a big body that weakens your own Tokens.

priest.name: Priest
priest.blurb: Priests channel their god into Smites. At the start of the game you Worship one of the four gods, and every priest of yours gets +3 on that god's side. Most priests conjure a Quarter Smite as they land, die or end your turn, and Smites combine for free in your hand: two Quarters make a Half, two Halves a Smite that destroys a Teece for a discard, two Smites a Divine Smite that destroys one outright. The High Priest and the Avatar can be paid for with Smites instead of bodies. Advanced, and one of the strongest decks in the box when the hand is managed well; the priests themselves are modest, and the hand limit of six is always pressing.
priest.lore: The Priesthood of the Four Sides worships the oldest gods in Teece: Topus of the top edge, Rightorious of the right, Bottomor of the bottom and Levt of the left, who between them hold the world in its frame. Their Temple stands at the heart of Middlemark, the one place equally far from all four, and directly on top of Gol’God’Oth, which is not a coincidence. The faithful fight hardest facing their god's direction, and a Smite is simply a prayer, concentrated. The Priests think the Paladins' three gods a passing fashion and the Warlocks thieves of divine power.
how: Worship: at the start of the game choose a god. Levt rules the left, Topus the top, Rightorious the right and Bottomor the bottom; all your priests get +3 on that side. A Prophet lets you switch. Worship belongs to the Priest deck: a priest the other side steals, or one drafted into another deck, gets no god.

Most priests conjure a Quarter Smite straight into your hand (a Teece gets -1 until the end of the turn). Two Quarters combine into a Half Smite (-5), two Halves into a Smite (discard a card: destroy a Teece), and two Smites into a Divine Smite (destroy a Teece, free). Combining uses the Combine button on the card and costs no play.
Smites count toward your hand limit of six, so combine or cast them before your turn ends. Divine Retribution counts as a Half Smite for combining, but held, it destroys whatever kills one of yours.

The High Priest and the Avatar can be paid for with Smites instead of bodies, and like the Devotee and the Votive Shield, they can be thrown away from your hand for one more Quarter Smite. Smite your own Teece through a Votive Shield to make it stronger.

dwarves.name: Dwarves
dwarves.blurb: Craftsmen who put everything into their gear. Eight equips stand in for magic and battlegrounds, and most dwarves read what they wear: Ranged, Flying, +4, or +5 Defence while equipped, and +3 for every piece on the Gear-Laden Recruit. Gear keeps coming back (the Tunnel Scavenger, the Delver and the Mountain King pull it out of the graveyard, and the Thane and the King take theirs home when they fall), so the plan is one juggernaut piled high and guarded by Mithril Mail, the Antimagic Airship and Ancestor's Aegis. Straightforward and sturdy; an unequipped dwarf is small, and anything that destroys equips or sends the juggernaut back to hand costs a great deal.
dwarves.lore: For countless millennia the Dwarves have perfected their craft in the caverns under the High Mountains, forging gear so good that whoever wears it hardly needs to be anyone at all. Their mines run straight through the Rock, which has led to a very long and very slow war, and they sell their surplus armour to the Knights at prices the Knights still complain about. The Soul of the Mountains was forged from a chip of the Rock God, and the Rock would like it back.
how: Eight equips stand in for magic and battlegrounds. Most dwarves read their own gear: Ranged, Flying, +4, or +5 Defence while equipped, or +3 for every equip on the Gear-Laden Recruit. The Deep Warden takes only one equip and doubles it.

Gear comes back. The Tunnel Scavenger and the Delver each pull an equip out of your graveyard into your hand, and the Mountain King equips two straight from the graveyard as it lands. The Thane and the King take their gear home to your hand when they fall.
Pile it onto one body. Heirloom Pauldrons pay +2 for every equip on their wearer, the Fresh-Forged Axe is plated onto a Teece still in your hand, and Ball and Chain goes on an enemy instead.

Protect the juggernaut: Mithril Mail adds +2 and +2 Defence, the Antimagic Airship floats clear of battlegrounds and soaks up the first enemy effect aimed at it, Ancestor’s Aegis keeps it alive through the next turn, and Soul of the Mountains leaves an Avalanche behind when it falls.

warlock.name: Warlock
warlock.blurb: Warlocks borrow their power from a patron, and every Teece you control carries the patron you are channelling: the Boon. Ten Warlocks each name a different patron (the Rock God, the Fey, the Devils, the Ogre God, the Old One, Zeus, the Bomb God, Ankhtepot, Nagash and Death), and calling one up changes what your whole side does, from +3 Defence to Flying to a stun on every arrival. The Adept and the Avatar let you hold several Boons at once, and Patron's Mark and the Patron's Shrine make one fire twice. Advanced and very flexible, with an answer for most boards; the Warlocks' own numbers are uneven, and it takes judgement to know which patron the turn needs.
warlock.lore: Warlocks are the gods' tenants. They keep their lease-market in the Sinking Sands, at the lip of the Pit, and rent power from any patron who will sign: the Rock God, the Fey, the Devils, the Ogre God, Zeus, the Bomb God, Ankhtepot, Nagash and Death, and, for the desperate, the Old One. The Priests call this theft and the Devils call it an excellent business opportunity. The Cult insists the Old One's real name is Gol’God’Oth, and that the Warlocks are behind on the rent.
how: The Boon: you channel one patron at a time, and every Teece you control has its effect. A Warlock that names a patron offers to switch the Boon as it lands. It is always optional, and the switch comes before its own when-played Boon fires, so a Warlock of Zeus can call Zeus and take his +5 at once.
A Warlock left on the field keeps a Channel button, once per turn, so you can swap back to its patron on a later turn without playing anything.

The Rock God gives +3 Defence, the Fey Flying, the Devils a PACT, the Ogre God a shove and a stun, the Old One +5 and Teleport whenever a card is discarded, Zeus +5 as it lands, the Bomb God and Ankhtepot an ability every turn, Nagash -3 to every enemy beside it, and Death cover for your next Teece when one falls. The Warlock’s Circle, when it goes, offers one more patron, the Circle, which draws a Lesser Circle under each Teece you play.

The Adept lets you hold three Boons at once while it stands, and the Avatar one more for the rest of the game. Patron's Mark and the Patron's Shrine add copies of the Boon, so it fires twice. Fickle Pact and the Pact Blade switch back to a patron you have used before, and Fickle Pact can also reach for one of the Priest's gods.
The Blessing changes with your patron, and fires once for every Boon you hold.

cult.name: Cult
cult.blurb: The Cult works to summon its god, Gol’God’Oth, and the whole board is its altar: a pentagram whose five points any Teece can Traverse between once a turn. Three missions run in order: light all five lines by walking them, cast the Convert they hand you to take a Teece beside one of yours, then end a turn with an ally in the middle panel, where it is sacrificed and a Tendril Of Gol’God’Oth rises, a Boss with 20 on every side. The Tendril is a Token, so it never counts toward winning, but it destroys almost anything beside it, and Gol’God’Oth Arrives copies it onto every empty panel around it. The cultists themselves are weak and the ritual is slow, so the god clears the way; the game is still won by holding the field.
cult.lore: The Cult of Gol’God’Oth meets in the cellars of Middlemark, as close to its god as the floor allows. It believes the nine panels are not a board at all but a pentagram, built over Gol’God’Oth to keep it asleep, and that the right lines lit in the right order will wake it. Gol’God’Oth is the thing the Warlocks politely call the Old One, and its whispering is what drove the Madness out of their minds. The Priests of the Four Sides pray on top of it, and the Wizards have sealed the middle panel twice, which the Cult considers extremely rude.
how: The Pentagram: the board is a pentagram whose five points are the top-middle, middle-left, middle-right, bottom-left and bottom-right panels. It shows through the Web and every battleground and cannot be removed or covered.

Traverse The Pentagram: once a turn, any Teece on a point, yours or the enemy’s, can teleport to one of the two points its lines reach, if that panel is empty. From the top-middle that is either bottom corner; from the bottom-right, the top-middle or the middle-left.

Three missions, in order. 1, Activate The Pentagram: travel along all five lines. A line an ally travels along glows red (an enemy traversing lights nothing) and stays lit, and all five hand you a Convert spell (take control of a Teece beside one of yours). 2, Convert The Enemy: cast it. Until you do, it comes back to your hand whenever it leaves. 3, Perform The Sacrifice: end your turn with an ally in the middle panel. It is sacrificed and a Tendril Of Gol’God’Oth with 20 on every side, a Boss, rises in its place.

Gol’God’Oth Arrives is the trump card: aimed at a Tendril it creates a copy of it on every empty panel beside it, aimed at anything else it sends that Teece back to its owner’s hand. Gol’God’Oth’s Boon lets you discard any card for +5 and Teleport, the Ley Nexus teleports to any point, and both light the lines they cross. The Pentagram and its missions belong to the Cult deck: with no Cult player in the game there is no Pentagram, so a cultist drafted into another deck cannot traverse.

paladin.name: Paladin
paladin.blurb: Paladins swear Oaths to one of three gods and fight harder while they keep them. Solitarius pays +4 to a Paladin that stands apart from its allies, Protectius +4 to every ally beside one, Pacificius +5 Defence to one that never kills; a broken Oath leaves the Paladin Oathbroken, with no bonus and -2. The Lights, the Vowkeeper and Glorious Redemption keep Oaths whole, the Paragon of the Three swears all three at once, and Cleanse lifts every curse, stun and penalty off an ally or strips an enemy bare. The Paladins are tiny until sworn, so the deck arranges the board around its Oaths, and anything that forces the wrong kind of contact breaks them.
paladin.lore: The Paladins serve the three gods of the Light, Solitarius, Protectius and Pacificius, young gods who broke away from the four Sides of the world over the question of what a Teece should do when it is not fighting. They keep their chapels on the snowline of the Hallowed North, as close to the Heavens as the old ways allow, and each Oath is a vow to one of the three answers. They have sworn to Cleanse every curse Ankhtepot's Mummies lay, they want their horses back from the Knights, and the Priests regard them as heretics with very good manners.
how: Oath: as a Paladin is played, swear it to a god. Solitarius gives it +4 but breaks when it becomes adjacent to an ally. Protectius gives every adjacent ally +4 and breaks when one of them dies. Pacificius gives it +5 Defence and breaks when it destroys an enemy. A broken Oath leaves the Paladin Oathbroken: no bonus, and -2.

Cleanse: on an ally it lifts every negative effect (stun, silence, curses, penalties); on an enemy it silences it and strips every bonus to its numbers. Devoathee Cleanses as it lands, and Holy Light's blessing Cleanses the whole cross around its Paladin each turn.

Keep Oaths whole: each Light equip is destroyed instead of its god's Oath breaking, the Vowkeeper's Oath never breaks, and Glorious Redemption swears a broken Paladin a new one. The Sentinel of Vows is destroyed by any Oath that does break, so play it where Oaths are safe.

The Celestial Steed and Ram carry their rider when it teleports or moves, and are destroyed at the end of a turn with a non-Paladin standing on them, so keep enemies off them. Sanctified Grounds gives your Teece in a 2x2 area +5 Defence until something in it falls.

knights.name: Knights
knights.blurb: Knights ride into battle on Mounts that lend them their numbers, their wings and their tricks. Every Knight is Armoured, with 1 Defence, and lands already riding the Mount printed on it, with the Mount's numbers and abilities on top of its own; bring the Knight down and its Mount is played on that panel or one next to it, ready for the next rider. Remount, Cavalry Muster and Call the Warhorse put spare Mounts on the board, the Stables guards them, and a Herd Saddle or a Mount Mount stacks several under one Knight. Hard to grind out, since every kill leaves a body behind; but the Knights alone are small, and a riderless Mount is a Token that never counts toward winning.
knights.lore: The mounted orders of the Wildwood marches, who hold from their castles at the forest's edge that a Teece is only as good as what it is sitting on. Their warhorses were bred from Celestial Steeds stolen from the Paladins, which the Paladins have never forgiven, and the Emu cavalry was a procurement error nobody will discuss. They buy their armour from the Dwarves, lend their officers to the Army, and take the credit for its victories.
how: Armoured: every Knight has 1 Defence. Mounts do not.

Mount: a Knight is played already riding the Mount printed on it and has the Mount’s numbers, Defence and abilities on top of its own. When the Knight is destroyed, its Mount is played on that panel or one next to it.

Play a Knight onto one of your Mounts on the board and it rides that Mount in place of its own. A Knight can have only one Mount, unless a Herd Saddle lets it keep both. Legaless can only be played onto a Mount.
A Mount standing on its own can, once per your turn, carry one of your Knights that has room for it: a Knight whose Mount was destroyed, or one wearing a Herd Saddle.

In hand, Dismount takes a Knight off its Mount, and the Mount becomes a card of its own: play it as a Teece, or tap it and then a Knight in hand with no Mount (Legaless included) to saddle it there, which costs no play.

Remount and Cavalry Muster put copies of Mounts on the board for the next Knights to ride; Stables makes a waiting Mount hard to kill, and the Armoury pays any equipped Teece, mounted Knights included.

angels.name: Angels
angels.blurb: Angels open the Heavens, three slots above the board, one over each column. While they are open, any Teece, yours or your opponent's, can be played up there instead of onto a panel, where nothing can fight it, and on a later turn it Descends down its column onto the first empty panel, usually gaining something as it lands. From the top row it can Ascend back up out of trouble. Angels are strong underneath and weak on top; some of them work from the sky (the Guardian Angel, the Watcher on High, the Angel of Mercy, the Messenger), and The Last Trumpet drops every one of them at once onto whatever stands below. Patient and hard to pin down, but slow to put Teece on the field.
angels.lore: The Host of Topus lives above the top edge, in the Heavens it shares with the Solar sky and Zeus's storm. Its nine choirs, one for every panel of the board, carry the top edge's word down to the world, which is why the Priests worship Topus and still find his messengers faintly embarrassing. The Host keeps its numbers at seven out of spite for the Devils of the Pit, who keep theirs at six, and an Angel that falls from the Heavens lands in the bottom row with a six on its sides and a contract waiting. The Solar orders tolerate the Angels as long as they stay out of the light, and Zeus is still deciding whether they count as weather.
how: The Heavens: three slots above the board, one per column. While an Angels deck is in the game, either player can play any Teece up there: tap it in hand and then tap an empty Heaven; that spends your Teece play. Up there it doesn't fight, counts toward nobody's field lead, can't be selected by any effect (you can still equip it), and is safe from whatever happens on the board.

Descend and Ascend: once per your turn, a Teece in the Heavens can drop down its column onto the first empty panel, but not on the turn it went up. Any Teece in the top row (or on a Cloudbank) can go back up into the empty Heaven above it. The Wheel of Eyes, Wings of Light and the Pearly Gates change where a Descent lands, and a Teece up there can pay for a Boss or Miniboss. Once per your turn, tap a Teece of yours in the Heavens to step it into an empty Heaven beside it.
Aim downward. An Angel's strong side is its Bottom, which faces whatever is below where it lands, so pick the column by what is under its first empty panel.

Work from the sky. The Guardian Angel takes a death for an ally below it, the Watcher on High weakens every enemy in its column, the Angel of Mercy gives its column Defence, and the Messenger swaps an ally up and out of danger. The Archangel of Topus goes back up into an empty Heaven whenever it is destroyed, and a Cherub lets an ally in the Heavens attack the Teece below it.

mimics.name: Mimics
mimics.blurb: Mimics are chests, bookcases, doors and wardrobes with teeth: the biggest bodies in the game, each with a catch that helps your opponent. A Bookcase hands them two cards when it falls or is sacrificed, a Front Door gives their next Teece +2, a Toy Chest summons two Tokens on their side. Play around the catch: silence your own Mimics with the Cushion, Play Dead, a Skeleton Key or the Haunted Manor, turn the gift round with a Looking Glass or let the Haunted Manor take an ally's gift for you.
mimics.lore: Mimics are what becomes of the things progress forgets. Down in the Badlands, among the lockers, safes and strongboxes nobody came back for, a chest left long enough in the dark starts to wait for a hand. They creep out into the rest of Teece dressed as treasure: a chest in a Dwarf vault, a wardrobe in a Middlemark inn, a door that was not there last week. Each one gives a little back as it is broken open, which is why treasure hunters keep going into rooms they should not, and the Hoard is what a Mimic becomes when it is left alone long enough with enough gold.
how: Every Mimic's drawback helps your opponent: a card drawn, a bonus on their next Teece, Tokens on their side, invulnerability. The numbers are huge to pay for it. Several drawbacks fire when the Mimic is sacrificed, too.

A silenced Mimic keeps its numbers and loses its drawback. The Cushion silences an ally when played and when discarded (and can be discarded from your hand on your turn), Play Dead and the Skeleton Key silence one, and the Haunted Manor silences every Teece left in your deck.

Turn the gift round. A Looking Glass turns your next gift round once, and discarding the Haunted Manor destroys an ally so that its when-destroyed effect comes to you. Even The Hoard, the Miniboss, pays out when it falls: the next magic card your opponent plays leaves a copy in their hand.

The Attic keeps a Teece invulnerable while it stands there, but marks it for good: when it is destroyed, the next Teece you play is destroyed as it lands. The Cursed Crown passes to whatever destroys its wearer, so you can destroy it once per turn rather than hand it over.

demons.name: Demons
demons.blurb: Demons fight from Hell. The deck opens a row of three Hell panels under the board, and anything that is not a Demon standing in Hell has -2, though Hell alone never takes a side below 0. Its cards turn more panels into Hell, drag enemies down into it, and pay Demons for standing there: the Lesser Demon and the Hellhound grow, the Tormentor bleeds the enemies beside it, and the Pit Sergeant and the Smoke Demon make Hell hard to dig them out of. Legion, the trump card, fills every empty Hell panel with Token copies of itself, and the Demon King turns the whole board into Hell. Big plain numbers, so a good first deck; the trick is choosing where the fight happens.
demons.lore: Under the bottom edge, past the Pit where the Devils keep their books, the board goes on burning. That is Hell, and the Demons live in it. The Devils will tell you the Demons are the help: they keep no contracts, read no fine print, and want nothing from a Teece but to drag it down where they are strong. Bottomor tolerates them because they keep the fires lit. Wherever a Demon stands for long enough, the ground under it remembers what it is, and the Angels above take this very personally.
how: Hell: three panels under the board, one under each column. They are real panels, so a Teece on one fights and counts for the lead. A non-Demon in Hell has -2, but Hell never takes a side below 0, and a battleground on a Hell panel negates Hell there unless the battleground says the panel is Hell.

Make more of it. The Brimstone Sower, the Hell Portal, Hell Breaks Loose, Brimstone Boots and both battlegrounds turn more panels into Hell; Satan's Little Helper makes the whole board Hell for a turn when it falls, and the Demon King for good.

Fight where you are strong. The Lesser Demon, the Hellhound, the Pitchfork and the Hellfire Bow only pay in Hell, the Tormentor only bites enemies standing in it, and the Pit Dragger pulls a Teece down its column when it falls.
Hold it. The Hellgate Warden keeps enemies from being played into Hell, the Smoke Demon hides your allies there from enemy effects, and the Pit Sergeant gives every Demon in Hell +2 Defence.

formats.name: Free-for-all
formats.blurb: Three separate sides. Everyone is your enemy, and the first side four Teece ahead of the next best wins.

formats.name: You and one computer
formats.blurb: You and the first computer fight as one side against the second. Allies never damage each other and win together.

formats.name: You against both
formats.blurb: Both computers are allied against you. Hardest of the three, and the reason the difficulty rating goes below zero.

map.name: The Heavens
map.text: Beyond the top edge, past Topus: the turning sky, the sun and moon, the storm, and the Host of Topus.

map.name: The Hallowed North
map.text: Snowfields and cloisters where the old ways meet the light. The Paladins keep their chapels on the snowline and the northern tribes roam below them.

map.name: The High Mountains
